Strategic Decision Focused Learning

Tinashe Handina ††thanks: Corresponding author: thandina@caltech.edu. Affiliation: California Institute of Technology    Yuehan Diao Affiliation: University of Chicago    Adam Wierman Affiliation: California Institute of Technology    Eric Mazumdar Affiliation: California Institute of Technology
Abstract

Machine learning (ML) predictions are increasingly being used to guide decision-making, giving rise to the problem of decision-focused learning (DFL) where predictors are optimized for downstream decision quality rather than accuracy alone. However, most existing work assumes a single decision-maker optimizing in isolation. This paper formalizes strategic decision-focused learning, where an ML system predicts an exogenous state that some agents observe before playing a game. For example, a park ranger may predict wildlife locations to allocate anti-poaching patrols against strategic poachers. While the exogenous state is unaffected by agent actions, predictions influence agents’ strategies and the resulting equilibrium. We find that strategic considerations fundamentally change the learning problem. In particular, we show the prediction accuracy–equilibrium payoff landscape can be non-monotonic—i.e., better predictions can degrade performance. We propose algorithmic approaches to address these challenges and validate them across benchmarks in wildlife conservation and infrastructure protection. Our theory and experiments highlight the importance of accounting for strategic interactions when designing predictors.

   

1 Introduction

Machine Learning (ML) systems are playing an increasingly vital role in shaping decisions across a wide range of domains. From commerce [4], to security [13] [28], to government [20] [34], decision makers are increasingly relying on the outputs of ML systems as the basis upon which they optimize their actions. Driving the proliferation of ML is its demonstrable ability to understand and predict the evolution of complex systems reasonably well. As ML systems become an ever more consequential tool used for decision making, understanding when standard training objectives are structurally inadequate — not merely suboptimal — is of vital importance. This paper identifies one such setting.

Learning with the view that the output of a learning algorithm is going to be used in a downstream optimization problem is an active area of research often called decision-focused learning[15][31][27]. Research in this area, to date, has often focused on a single decision maker leveraging ML outputs to optimize a utility or cost function in isolation [27]. In many consequential applications, however, decision makers find that they are interacting with other actors who often act in a strategic manner. This introduces complexities to the optimization problem as the agent now not only has to consider the impact of the decision on the cost function, but also has to take into account how other actors may respond to any particular decision they make.

In this work, we formalize this problem area which we call strategic decision-focused learning (SDFL). In this setting, an agent is trying to leverage ML systems to aid with the prediction of some exogenous state that affects a game that they play. Such settings are prevalent across a wide range of domains, including:

  • •

    Electricity markets: ML predictors can be used by producers competing in grid markets to forecast exogenous renewable generation conditions (e.g., wind and solar availability), which are then used to inform pricing strategies that interact with those of competing producers.

  • •

    Motorsport strategy: In Formula One, teams leverage predictive models to forecast exogenous variables such as tire degradation rates and safety car probabilities, which shape pit-stop and fuel strategies in direct competition with opposing teams.

  • •

    Security and conservation: Predicting population distributions over a geographic region — such as wildlife density or civilian movement — informs patrol strategies in adversarial security games (we evaluate this concretely in conservation and infrastructure protection domains in this work).

We find that the explicit characterization of the downstream strategic interaction leads to fundamental — not merely practical — considerations for the design and use of machine learning systems. To that end, this work seeks to address the following question:

How should agents develop and make use of Machine Learning for exogenous state predictions in strategic interactions?

Traditional approaches to this problem in the strategic domain have often relied on first predicting exogenous states such as demand [29] or population distributions [26], then optimizing for a decision. We show that this approach is not merely suboptimal but also suffers from a fundamental issue of misalignment. As we show, in strategic settings no monotone transformation of a supervised accuracy loss can serve as a reliable proxy for strategic utility. This failure is structural, arising from the interaction between prediction error and equilibrium response, and persists regardless of model capacity or data quantity.

Our contributions: This paper makes three conceptual contributions and one algorithmic contribution.

(C1) Problem formalization. We formalize strategic decision-focused learning as a distinct problem within the decision-focused learning paradigm. The SDFL problem is defined for general games and solution concepts: an agent predicts an exogenous state and commits to an equilibrium strategy based on that prediction, while opponents respond under the true state. This split between the predicted world the agent plans for and the true world opponents respond to is the source of all the difficulty we characterize. The Stackelberg equilibrium is one tractable instantiation we study in depth; the formalization and hardness results hold for general solution concepts.

(C2) Structural hardness. We prove that the mapping from prediction accuracy to equilibrium payoff is provably non-monotone: a less accurate prediction can strictly outperform a more accurate one (Proposition 3.2), while the true state in, some instances, may be suboptimal (Proposition 3.3). Together, these results characterize the structure of the accuracy–utility landscape. This is not a worst-case pathology: it is a feature of the landscape, implying that standard predict-then-optimize pipelines are not well motivated for SDFL.

(C3) Geometric characterization of hardness. We prove that, for a class of games, as game dimensionality grows, an increasing proportion of strategies lie near best-response boundaries (Theorem 3.7), explaining geometrically why small prediction errors may induce large utility swings. This result characterizes why the hardness can intensify as the action space grows.

(C4) Initial algorithmic framework. Motivated by C1–C3, we propose end-to-end prediction approaches as an initial algorithmic response to SDFL. We present these as proof-of-concept rather than definitive solutions, in the same spirit as early task-loss surrogates in single-agent DFL that preceded formal analysis [3, 31]. Experiments across two real-world security game domains validate that end-to-end approaches outperform predict-then-optimize despite higher supervised prediction error, corroborating our theoretical findings that accuracy and strategic utility are misaligned.

1.1 Related work

Learning how to make use of machine learning for the purposes of downstream decision making has emerged as an important area of research [15, 5]. The key idea powering much of this work is that embedding the optimization problem of interest into the training loop and backpropagating decision-relevant gradients can lead to better performance than first optimizing a prediction and then optimizing for a decision [3, 33]. While standard approaches to decision-focused learning often focus on a single agent optimizing in isolation [27], we focus on extending and formalizing this paradigm for the strategic domain. In particular, we consider what happens when the decision is observed by strategic agents whose choices are affected by the optimization decision itself. We call this setting strategic decision-focused learning. Crucially, the strategic setting is not merely a harder instance of standard DFL but a qualitatively different problem: the accuracy–utility misalignment we identify has no analogue in the single-agent case. Closest to our work is game-focused learning in security games [24, 30]: there the payoffs are known, and a defender learns how an attacker reacts and then best-responds to what is learned. In our framework, the state that sets the payoffs, which our opponents already observe, is what is predicted. The predictor then plays an equilibrium of the game it thinks it is in. This introduces new forms of complexity: for example, predicting the true state in some instances may be suboptimal (Proposition 3.3).

Learning in strategic environments:

Recent years have seen a surge of research on deploying learning algorithms within strategic environments [17, 16]. This focus on the intersection of learning and strategic interactions has given rise to, among others, the domains of strategic classification [11], adversarial machine learning [14], and multi-agent reinforcement learning [35]. Closely related is performative prediction [23], wherein the act of prediction itself causes a distributional shift in the data the model is trained on. Our work takes an orthogonal track: rather than the prediction changing the input distribution, we ask how to properly account for exogenous state information within a strategic decision-making task where the prediction shapes the equilibrium that emerges. The exogeneity of the data distribution is what separates SDFL from performative prediction; the presence of strategic opponents is what separates it from standard DFL. A key theme arising from this body of work is that learning in strategic environments is often non-trivial, with phenomena such as instability of algorithms resulting in convergence to cycles and chaos [18], and strategic manipulations leading to improved causal discovery [1]. Of particular interest is the insight that small changes in learning parameters may lead to different equilibria with different utilities [36]. Previous work has also found that model selection within the broader context of learning in strategic environments is complicated, with the model expressivity–payoff landscape in general being non-monotonic [10]. Our work contributes a precise characterization of this non-monotonicity in the SDFL setting, grounding it in the geometry of best-response regions rather than model expressivity.

2 Problem Formulation

We formalize strategic decision-focused learning as a distinct problem within the decision-focused learning paradigm. We begin with a general formulation applicable to any game and solution concept, then instantiate it for the Stackelberg setting we study in depth.

In the standard decision-focused learning (DFL) setting, a single agent uses a learned model fθ:𝒳→𝒮f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S} to predict an uncertain parameter s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and solves a downstream optimization problem whose objective depends on ss. The central insight of DFL is that training fθf_{\theta} to minimize a supervised loss can be suboptimal when downstream decision quality is what matters [5, 31]. Critically, most existing DFL assumes the agent optimizes in isolation — no other agent observes or responds to the decision. As we show, this isolation assumption is not merely a simplification but a load-bearing one: its violation changes the learning problem qualitatively.

2.1 Strategic Decision-Focused Learning

We consider a game G=(𝒩,{𝒜i}i∈𝒩,{Ui}i∈𝒩,𝒮)G=(\mathcal{N},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\{U_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\mathcal{S}) where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a finite set of agents, 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} is the action set of agent ii, 𝒮⊆ℝd\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is an exogenous state space, and Ui:∏j𝒜j×𝒮→ℝU_{i}:\prod_{j}\mathcal{A}_{j}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} is agent ii’s utility. Each agent selects a mixed strategy αi∈Δ⁡(𝒜i)\alpha_{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{i}).

The state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} is exogenous: drawn from a fixed distribution P𝒮P_{\mathcal{S}} independently of any agent’s actions. A primary agent ii observes only a dataset 𝒟={(x(t),s(t))}t=1T\mathcal{D}=\{(x^{(t)},s^{(t)})\}_{t=1}^{T} and learns a predictor fθ:𝒳→𝒮f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}. All other agents observe the true realized state srs_{r}.

Let σ:𝒮→∏jΔ⁡(𝒜j)\sigma:\mathcal{S}\to\prod_{j}\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{j}) denote a solution mapping returning an equilibrium profile for a given state. Agent ii commits to σi​(s^)\sigma_{i}(\hat{s}) based on their prediction s^=fθ​(x)\hat{s}=f_{\theta}(x), while opponents respond under the true state srs_{r}. The realized joint profile is: σ⁡(s^,sr)=(σi​(s^),Eq−i​(σi​(s^),sr))\sigma(\hat{s},s_{r})=\big(\sigma_{i}(\hat{s}),\;\mathrm{Eq}_{-i}(\sigma_{i}(\hat{s}),\;s_{r})\big) where Eq−i​(αi,s)\mathrm{Eq}_{-i}(\alpha_{i},s) is the equilibrium response of agents −i-i to a fixed αi\alpha_{i} under state ss. The strategic decision-focused learning problem is then:

θ∗=arg⁡maxθ​𝔼(x,sr)∼𝒟​[Ui​(σ⁡(fθ​(x),sr),sr)]\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,s_{r})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[U_{i}\!\left(\sigma(f_{\theta}(x),\,s_{r}),\;s_{r}\right)\right] (1)

The split between the predicted world agent ii plans for and the true world opponents respond to is the source of all the difficulty we characterize in Section 3. We note that this formulation is distinct from performative prediction [23], wherein predictions shift P𝒮P_{\mathcal{S}} through a feedback loop — here the data distribution is fixed and predictions affect only the equilibrium. Our framework is clearly distinguished from existing learning problems in Figure 1.

2.2 Stackelberg Instantiation

The SDFL objective equation 1 is defined for general games and solution concepts; the hardness results of Section 3 hold in this generality. For the algorithmic contributions and experiments of Sections 4, we instantiate SDFL under the Stackelberg solution concept, chosen for tractability and its natural fit to security applications.

We focus on two-player interactions in which agent ii leads and agent −i-i follows. Given predicted state s^\hat{s}, the leader computes: α¯i​(s^)=arg⁡maxαi∈Δ⁡(𝒜i)​Ui​(αi,B​R−i​(αi,s^),s^)\bar{\alpha}_{i}(\hat{s})=\arg\max_{\alpha_{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{i})}U_{i}\!\left(\alpha_{i},\;BR_{-i}(\alpha_{i},\hat{s}),\;\hat{s}\right) where B​R−i​(αi,s)=arg⁡maxα−i​U−i​(αi,α−i,s)BR_{-i}(\alpha_{i},s)=\arg\max_{\alpha_{-i}}U_{-i}(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{-i},s). Since the follower responds under the true state srs_{r}, the leader’s realized utility is: Uirealized​(s^,sr)=Ui​(α¯i​(s^),B​R−i​(α¯i​(s^),sr),sr)U_{i}^{\mathrm{realized}}(\hat{s},s_{r})=U_{i}\!\left(\bar{\alpha}_{i}(\hat{s}),\;BR_{-i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}(\hat{s}),\;s_{r}),\;s_{r}\right). Stackelberg equilibria are the natural solution concept for security settings, where attackers are assumed to observe both the state and the defender’s committed strategy [32].

Illustrative example.

A game ranger predicts elephant locations to allocate patrols against strategic poachers. The exogenous state — the true elephant distribution — is unknown to the ranger but (in the worst case) observed by the poachers. The ranger commits to a patrol strategy based on their prediction; the poachers best-respond knowing the truth. The ranger’s realized utility depends not on how accurately they predicted elephant locations, but on how well their patrol strategy performs against opponents who know the true state. This gap between prediction quality and strategic performance is precisely what equation 1 captures.

3 Limitations of Accuracy based Predictions in Games

We establish that standard accuracy-based approaches to SDFL suffer from a problem of mis-alignment. We prove two independent results that together characterize why: first, the mapping from prediction accuracy to equilibrium payoff is provably non-monotone, implying no monotone transformation of a supervised loss can serve as a reliable proxy for strategic utility; second, for a broad class of games, the fraction of strategies near best-response boundaries grows with game dimensionality, explaining geometrically why small prediction errors induce large utility swings. While we instantiate these results in the Stackelberg setting for concreteness, the non-monotonicity result holds for the general SDFL objective equation 1 under other solution mappings, σ\sigma, satisfying the conditions of Section 2.

Given a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} relating to the exogenous state ss, standard approaches to learning in strategic environments first find some sp​r​e​ds_{pred} by minimizing a statistical loss function ℒ⁡(ϕ,𝒟)\mathcal{L}(\phi,\mathcal{D}) which is proportional to some accuracy metric ϕ\phi for the game instance. After having learned a prediction of the state, the agent then looks to optimize their decision-making given their state prediction, which was yielded from the previous estimation step.

Definition 3.1 (Accuracy Metric).

Let 𝒮⊆ℝn\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and let sr∈𝒮s_{r}\in\mathcal{S} be the true realization of the state. An accuracy metric for the game instance is a function ϕ:𝒮→ℝ≥0\phi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} defined by ϕ⁡(s)=‖s−sr‖\phi(s)=\|s-s_{r}\| for some symmetric norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

To extend the previous example of elephant conservation, we assume that the ranger is given some dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} on the location of elephants within the reserve. Standard approaches to the strategic decision-focused learning problem would have the ranger find sp​r​e​ds_{pred} (a prediction of where the elephants would be), and then from there, they would optimize to find a patrol strategy that maximizes their utility. We call this approach to learning “Predict Then Optimize” (PTO).

We begin by showing the limitations of this particular learning paradigm. We find that it is possible for a state prediction to be less accurate yet lead the decision maker into selecting an action that yields better payoff when compared to some other, more accurate state prediction. This shows that utility within the context of strategic environments can be non-monotonic with respect to prediction accuracy.

Proposition 3.2.

There exists a game instance with true state srs_{r}, and predictions sp,1s_{p,1} and sp,2s_{p,2}, wherein sp,1s_{p,1} is strictly more accurate than sp,2s_{p,2} under every accuracy metric ϕ\phi, yet player ii’s utility at the equilibrium induced by sp,1s_{p,1} is strictly lower than that induced by sp,2s_{p,2}:

Ui​(α∗​(sp,1),sr)<Ui​(α∗​(sp,2),sr),U_{i}\!\left(\alpha^{*}(s_{p,1}),\,s_{r}\right)\;<\;U_{i}\!\left(\alpha^{*}(s_{p,2}),\,s_{r}\right),

where α∗​(s)=(αi∗​(s),B​R−i​(αi∗​(s),sr))\alpha^{*}(s)=(\alpha_{i}^{*}(s),\,BR_{-i}(\alpha_{i}^{*}(s),s_{r})) denotes the equilibrium joint strategy profile when the primary plays assuming state ss, the rest of the agents see the true state srs_{r}, and utility is evaluated at srs_{r}.

In addition, we find that there exist game instances in which the true state srs_{r} is not the utility-optimal prediction for a player: a strategically calibrated misprediction can induce an equilibrium that, when played against the true state, yields strictly higher utility than the equilibrium induced by srs_{r} itself.

Proposition 3.3.

There exists a game instance with true state srs_{r} and player ii such that there exists a prediction sp∈𝒮s_{p}\in\mathcal{S} satisfying:

Ui​(α∗​(sp),sr)>Ui​(α∗​(sr),sr),U_{i}\!\left(\alpha^{*}(s_{p}),\,s_{r}\right)\;>\;U_{i}\!\left(\alpha^{*}(s_{r}),\,s_{r}\right),

where α∗​(s)=(αi∗​(s),B​R−i​(αi∗​(s),sr))\alpha^{*}(s)=(\alpha_{i}^{*}(s),\,BR_{-i}(\alpha_{i}^{*}(s),s_{r})) denotes the equilibrium joint strategy profile when the primary plays assuming state ss, the rest of the agents see the true state srs_{r}, and utility is evaluated at srs_{r}.

The case for utility-aware approaches in games is further strengthened by the general volatility of the strategy-utility landscape. In particular, we see that for a wide characterization of games, the probability that a uniformly sampled strategy is near another strategy with a different best response increases with the dimensionality of the game. This phenomenon points to why, in some instances, small perturbations in state predictions result in completely different utilities.

Definition 3.4.

Let A,BA,B be two players in a bi-matrix game G=(A, B)G=(\textbf{A, B}). For player AA, we define the best response region for each action bb of player BB to be RbA:={α∈Δ⁡(𝒜)|b∈B​R​(α)}R_{b}^{A}:=\{\alpha\in\Delta({\mathcal{A}})|b\in BR(\alpha)\}.

Definition 3.5.

We say that a particular strategy α∈RbA\alpha\in R^{A}_{b} is δ−\delta-regional if ∃α′∈Rb′A\exists\alpha^{\prime}\in R^{A}_{b^{\prime}} with b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime} such that ‖α−α′‖2≤δ\|\alpha-\alpha^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\delta.

In the above definitions, we formally describe best response regions (i.e., collections of strategies that elicit the same best response from a follower) and δ\delta-regional strategies (strategies that, despite belonging to a particular best response region, are very close to another best response region). We seek to understand the prevalence of δ−\delta-regional strategies.

Assumption 3.6.

Let {GN}N=2∞\{G_{N}\}_{N=2}^{\infty} be a sequence of two-player bi-matrix games in which both players have NN actions, indexed by [N]={1,…,N}[N]=\{1,\dots,N\}. For each action b∈[N]b\in[N] for player BB, the best-response region for player AA, RbA,(N)R_{b}^{A,(N)}, is such that (1) RbA,(N)≠∅R_{b}^{A,(N)}\neq\emptyset and (2) for all α∈RbA,(N)\alpha\in R_{b}^{A,(N)}, we have αb≥2​δN\alpha_{b}\geq 2\delta_{N}, where αb\alpha_{b} denotes the probability that player AA’s mixed strategy α\alpha places on its bb-th action and {δN}\{\delta_{N}\} is a sequence of positive numbers.

We briefly remark on the strength of these conditions. Condition (1) simply requires that no player BB action is strictly dominated—that is, every action in the player BB’s action set is a best response to some player AA mixed strategy. This is a mild non-degeneracy requirement.

Condition (2) is more substantive but natural in a broad class of games. It asks that whenever player BB’s best response is action bb, player AA places at least probability 2​δN2\delta_{N} on their own action bb. Since the numbering of actions is arbitrary, the condition need only hold under some permutation. In security game formulations, for instance, the permutation pairs each attacker action bb with a defender action σ⁡(b)\sigma(b), and the condition reduces to requiring that each attacked cell is driven by the defender’s commitment to patrolling some corresponding location—a mild structural requirement.

Theorem 3.7.

Suppose the sequence of games {GN}N=2∞\{G_{N}\}_{N=2}^{\infty} satisfies Assumption 3.6 with δN=c/N\delta_{N}=c/N for some c∈(0,12]c\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}]. For each NN, let α∼Unif⁡(Δ⁡(𝒜))\alpha\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\Delta(\mathcal{A})) in game GNG_{N}, then:

ℙ⁡(α​ is ​δN​-regional)≥ 1−(1−c​2N)N−1.\mathbb{P}\!\big(\alpha\text{ is }\delta_{N}\text{-regional}\big)\;\geq\;1-\left(1-\frac{c\sqrt{2}}{N}\right)^{\!N-1}.

Theorem 3.7 illustrates how volatility naturally arises in games. For games satisfying Assumption 3.6, a uniformly sampled leader strategy is δN\delta_{N}-regional with probability at least 1−(1−c​2N)N−11-\left(1-\frac{c\sqrt{2}}{N}\right)^{N-1}. This bound increases with NN and has the non-vanishing limit 1−e−c​21-e^{-c\sqrt{2}}, which is approximately 0.5070.507 at c=12c=\tfrac{1}{2}. As the dimensionality of the game grows, small perturbations to the leader’s strategy may therefore suffice to change the follower’s response. This susceptibility to downstream disruption is precisely what motivates a decision-focused approach.

Remark 3.8.

Theorem 3.7 bounds the prevalence of near-boundary strategies in strategy space; it makes no statement about utilities. Two steps connect it to utilities: a small change in the prediction can move the induced strategy across a best-response boundary, and where adjacent regions carry different leader utilities the realized utility then can change sharply. Games with such utility differences across adjacent regions are possible.

4 End to End Predictions in Strategic Settings

The results of Section 3 establish that no accuracy-based training objective can serve as a reliable proxy for strategic utility. This motivates a fundamentally different approach to learning in the SDFL setting, which we call End-To-End (ETE) prediction selection: rather than optimizing for predictive accuracy in isolation, ETE directly targets the downstream strategic objective. We present this framework as an initial algorithmic response to SDFL — a proof of concept demonstrating tractability rather than a definitive solution, in the same spirit as early end-to-end approaches in single-agent DFL that preceded formal convergence analysis [3, 31].

Formally, let fθ:𝒳→𝒮f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S} be a parameterized model mapping observable features x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} (derived from dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}) to a predicted state fθ​(x)∈𝒮f_{\theta}(x)\in\mathcal{S}. The ETE problem is to find parameters θ∗\theta^{*} that maximize the leader’s realized utility at equilibrium as per equation 1. This objective is challenging to optimize directly: the true state, srs_{r}, is unobserved at training time, and the mapping θ↦Ui​(⋅)\theta\mapsto U_{i}(\cdot) passes through an equilibrium computation that is in general non-differentiable in θ\theta.

In the Stackelberg setting, this non-differentiability is concrete: α¯ifθ​(x)\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{f_{\theta}(x)} is the solution to a linear program (LP) whose payoff matrices are determined by fθ​(x)f_{\theta}(x), and the LP argmax is non-smooth. Moreover, by Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.7, the objective is neither monotone in prediction accuracy nor smooth in θ\theta, so optimizing a supervised proxy is unreliable. These challenges motivate a two-stage development. We first consider the case where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is discrete and finite: here, utility can be evaluated exactly for any candidate prediction, which isolates the algorithmic question of how to search over predictions by strategic utility. We then turn to the general continuous setting, where both sources of difficulty are present.

4.1 Warm-up: End to End State Prediction with Discrete, Finite State Spaces

A core principle of ETE is that candidate predictions should be evaluated by the strategic utility they induce, not solely by statistical accuracy. A good ETE algorithm must therefore explore candidate predictions and filter them by downstream performance. We begin by showing this explore-then-filter principle is sound. In the discrete, finite-state setting, bandit-style approaches such as successive elimination can enumerate candidate predictions and evaluate each by its induced utility. We show that the cumulative cost of exploring suboptimal predictions is sublinear in TT, even when the equilibrium induced by each candidate must itself be learned (provided per-state equilibrium computation is also sublinear in TT).

Theorem 4.1.

Consider a game GG with a finite set of exogenous states, and let srs_{r} denote the true realized state. Let αi,ts\alpha_{i,t}^{s} denote the strategy selected by player ii at time step tt given state prediction ss produced by algorithm 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG}, and let (α¯is,α¯−is)(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s}) be the unique equilibrium joint strategy profile given prediction state ss. Suppose utilities are bounded, i.e. Ui​(⋅,⋅,s)∈[0,1]U_{i}(\cdot,\cdot,s)\in[0,1] for all ss. If

𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢​(s)​[∑t=1T|Ui​(αi,ts,α−i,ts,s′)−Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,s′)|]∈o⁡(T)∀fixed ​(s,s′),\underset{\mathcal{ALG}(s)}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s},s^{\prime})-U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s^{\prime})\bigr|\right]\in o(T)\quad\forall\,\text{fixed }(s,s^{\prime}),

then 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}, which combines 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG} with successive elimination to determine an evaluation state, yields:

𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′​[∑t=1T|Ui​(αi,tst,α−i,tst,sr)−maxs∈𝒮⁡Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,sr)|]∈o⁡(T).\underset{\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s_{t}},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s_{t}},s_{r})-\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\,U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s_{r})\right|\right]\in o(T).

4.2 End-to-End Prediction in General Settings

The warm-up setting assumes a finite, discrete state space and allows repeated evaluations of the same state. These luxuries rarely hold in practice. In general applications, the state space is continuous or combinatorially large, and we are given a dataset from which we are to return a single model for state prediction. In this paradigm, we are therefore unable to directly apply bandit-style enumeration. We thus seek an approach that retains the core principle of evaluating candidate predictions via their downstream strategic utility within a single-pass learning framework.

The theory above presents two concrete challenges for optimizing in the SDFL domain. Firstly, Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 establish that the mapping θ↦Uirealized\theta\mapsto U_{i}^{\text{realized}} is fundamentally misaligned with accuracy-based surrogates. This renders approaches such as gradient descent on prediction error alone insufficient. Secondly, Theorem 3.7 establishes that strategies close to a best-response boundary grow increasingly prevalent as game dimensionality increases; where adjacent regions carry different leader utilities, the utility landscape is discontinuous across the boundary. We therefore derive a heuristic tailored to the discontinuous optimization landscape induced by strategic responses in SDFL problems.

Algorithm 1 addresses these challenges by combining three ideas. First, we perform intra-region optimization within regions where the strategic response is fixed, using KKT-directed gradients that exploit differentiability within a fixed best-response zone to directly optimize through the follower’s best response. Within these strategic epochs, the Huber regularisation weight λe\lambda_{e} is annealed from λmax\lambda_{\max} to λmin\lambda_{\min}, keeping prediction quality grounded in early KKT steps when the strategic gradient would otherwise dominate and destabilize training. Second, we perform inter-region exploration to optimize across best-response regions via supervised updates, which shift the induced leader strategy across zone boundaries. A strategic checkpoint filter, motivated by the explore-then-filter principle of Theorem 4.1, selects across candidates produced by both mechanisms to navigate the globally non-convex and discontinuous landscape.

KKT-directed gradients.

Given a predicted state sp​r​e​ds_{pred}, the leader’s optimal strategy α¯i\bar{\alpha}_{i} solves a linear program whose KKT conditions form a differentiable system in α¯i\bar{\alpha}_{i} and the payoff parameters. For a fixed follower pure action a−ia_{-i}, implicit differentiation yields ∂α¯i/∂sp​r​e​d\partial\bar{\alpha}_{i}/\partial s_{pred}, enabling backpropagation of strategic utility to θ\theta. However, as Theorem 3.7 predicts, near best-response boundaries the follower’s action switches discontinuously, and the KKT gradient—derived with a−ia_{-i} fixed—becomes unreliable. This motivates alternation: odd regimes apply supervised updates with Gaussian input perturbations to traverse Δ⁡(𝒜i)\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{i}) and escape boundary regions, while even regimes apply 𝒰KKT\mathcal{U}_{\text{KKT}} where the gradient is well-defined.

Strategic checkpoint filter.

At the close of every regime of RR epochs—whether a supervised or KKT regime—the current parameters θ\theta are evaluated on a held-out set 𝒟eval\mathcal{D}_{\text{eval}} via the strategic utility function 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and accepted only if they improve upon the best recorded utility u∗u^{*}; otherwise training reverts to θ∗\theta^{*}. This mechanism is motivated in part by Theorem 4.1: we identify model parameters by evaluating them for their downstream strategic utility.

Remark 4.2.

The checkpoint filter selects a model whose expected strategic utility is within ε\varepsilon of the best candidate: 𝒰⁡(θ∗)≥max1≤k≤K⁡𝒰⁡(θk)−ε\mathcal{U}(\theta^{*})\geq\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathcal{U}(\theta_{k})-\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, provided |𝒟eval|≥2​ln⁡(2​K/δ)/ε2|\mathcal{D}_{\text{eval}}|\geq 2\ln(2K/\delta)/\varepsilon^{2}. This follows from standard arguments using Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over the K=⌈T/R⌉K=\lceil T/R\rceil checkpoints.

4.3 Experimental Evaluation: Security Games

Building on game-theoretic approaches to security [25, 8, 13], we instantiate two Stackelberg security games on an N×NN\!\times\!N grid GG: a conservation game using GPS tracks of 15 African elephants in Etosha National Park [9], and an infrastructure game using ridership data from 123 Manhattan subway stations (Jan 2022–Dec 2024) [19]. In both, a defender commits to a mixed strategy αi∈Δ⁡(G)\alpha_{i}\in\Delta(G) over patrol allocations, and an attacker who observes this commitment chooses α−i∈Δ⁡(G)\alpha_{-i}\in\Delta(G) [32]. The exogenous state s∈ℤ+Ns\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{N} captures the value at risk per cell: uncontested attacks cost the defender utility proportional to the cell value nn (and reward the attacker proportionally), successful interdiction rewards the defender proportionally and penalizes the attacker by a fixed amount, and unvisited cells contribute zero. Full details are in Appendix B.

4.3.1 Methodology

We frame the problem as supervised regression: given temporal and historical features for each cell in GG, predict the scalar value (elephant count or ridership) at a future period. All methods share a common base neural network architecture; comprehensive details on implementation, feature engineering, and training are in Appendix B.

Results.

We compare four methods. PTO minimizes predictive loss and feeds the resulting prediction directly to the Stackelberg LP. The three ETE variants differ in how strategic information enters training. ZOC (Zeroth-Order Checkpoint) trains on supervised loss but applies a strategic checkpoint filter after each regime, retaining only parameters that improve utility on 𝒟eval\mathcal{D}_{\text{eval}}. KKT differentiates through the Stackelberg LP via KKT conditions, backpropagating strategic utility directly to model parameters. Hybrid (Algorithm 1) alternates supervised and KKT regimes with the checkpoint filter applied after each. We evaluate on two axes: Mean Absolute Error MAE=1N​|𝒯|​∑t∈𝒯∑i∈[N]|y^ti−yti|\mathrm{MAE}=\frac{1}{N|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i\in[N]}|\hat{y}^{i}_{t}-y^{i}_{t}| and downstream strategic utility across all evaluation instances. Table 1 reports both metrics at 500 epochs—the budget at which all methods converged—across both game environments. Utility is averaged over all evaluation instances (396 daily instances for conservation, 1098 for infrastructure) and 5 independent training runs; MAE is computed analogously. Figure 2 shows the same utilities month by month over each test period.

PTO, on average, achieves lower MAE than all ETE approaches, indicating superior predictive accuracy in the conventional supervised learning sense. However, this advantage does not translate into better strategic outcomes: all three ETE methods achieve higher defender utility than PTO in both domains. Critically, Hybrid achieves the best strategic utility across both game environments — outperforming not only PTO but also ZOC and KKT in isolation — demonstrating that combining supervised exploration, KKT-directed gradients, and the strategic checkpoint filter yields consistent gains that neither component delivers on its own.

Figure 3 illustrates the instance-level dynamics underlying these aggregate results. The utility landscape is complex and volatile—consistent with Theorem 3.7—and no single method universally dominates at the individual instance level. In instances where ETE methods outperform PTO, the ETE predictions better capture strategically relevant structure in the state, even at the cost of raw predictive accuracy. We illustrate such instances in the above figure. To probe the general landscape and gain an understanding of how in some cases we may see variation with PTO approaches, we include a 100 action synthetic setting on a grid with multiple modes in Appendix B.1: here we illustrate how different state representations produce distinct downstream strategic consequences.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we formalized strategic decision-focused learning as a distinct problem within the decision-focused learning paradigm, targeting settings where ML predictions are consumed by strategically interacting agents. We showed that prediction accuracy and strategic payoff can be non-monotonic, motivating a departure from predict-then-optimize pipelines, and proposed an end-to-end framework that incorporates downstream strategic utility directly into model selection via KKT-directed gradients and strategic evaluation on a held-out partition.

Several important directions remain open. Our formulation assumes followers observe the true state; modeling settings in which followers must also learn the state from data introduces a second layer of strategic complexity worth exploring. More broadly, precisely characterizing the conditions under which equilibrium-aware end-to-end approaches outperform predict-then-optimize, and developing scalable algorithms for this regime, are promising avenues for future work.

Appendix

Limitations and Broader Impact

Limitations.

Our formulation assumes that followers observe the true state of the world; in practice, followers may also need to learn the state from data, introducing a second layer of strategic complexity that our framework does not capture. We provide a local non-monotonicity result motivating end-to-end training, but a precise characterization of when equilibrium-aware approaches outperform predict-then-optimize remains open.

Broader impact.

Strategic decision-focused learning is motivated by settings where a decision-maker deploys ML predictions against agents who respond strategically — a structure common in security, infrastructure allocation, and market design. Improved patrol allocation in conservation and transit safety are positive applications, but the same framework could in principle be used in ways that raise fairness and civil-liberties concerns.

Proof of Proposition 3.3.

We follow the proof structure and argument of Theorem 3.4 in [10]. We work in the following setting: we have a two-player continuous game in which the primary agent (player ii) has strategy space from a compact set 𝒜i⊆ℝ\mathcal{A}_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R} and the opposing agent (player −i-i) has strategy space from a compact set 𝒜−i⊆ℝ\mathcal{A}_{-i}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}, with utilities Ui​(αi,α−i,s)U_{i}(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{-i},s) and U−i​(αi,α−i,s)U_{-i}(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{-i},s) respectively. The exogenous state space 𝒮={0,1}\mathcal{S}=\{0,1\}. We assume the following.

Assumption A.1.

Restatement of Theorem  3.7. Suppose the sequence of games {GN}N=2∞\{G_{N}\}_{N=2}^{\infty} satisfies Assumption 3.6 with δN=c/N\delta_{N}=c/N for some c∈(0,12]c\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}]. For each NN, let α∼Unif⁡(Δ⁡(𝒜))\alpha\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\Delta(\mathcal{A})) in game GNG_{N}, then:

ℙ⁡(α​ is ​δN​-regional)≥ 1−(1−c​2N)N−1.\mathbb{P}\!\big(\alpha\text{ is }\delta_{N}\text{-regional}\big)\;\geq\;1-\left(1-\frac{c\sqrt{2}}{N}\right)^{\!N-1}.
Proof of Theorem 3.7.

We instantiate the geometric arguments of [21] to our context. The conditions of Assumption 3.6 ensure that the best-response regions {RbA,(N)}b∈[N]\{R^{A,(N)}_{b}\}_{b\in[N]} form a Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz (KKM) covering [12] of the simplex Δ⁡(𝒜)\Delta(\mathcal{A}). Let μN−1\mu_{N-1} denote the (N−1)(N{-}1)-dimensional Lebesgue measure on Δ⁡(𝒜)\Delta(\mathcal{A}).

Define S=⋃b≠b′(RbA,(N)∩Rb′A,(N))S=\bigcup_{b\neq b^{\prime}}(R^{A,(N)}_{b}\cap R^{A,(N)}_{b^{\prime}}) and its δN\delta_{N}-neighborhood SδN={α∈Δ(𝒜):∃α′∈S,∥α−α′∥2≤δN}S_{\delta_{N}}=\{\alpha\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}):\exists\,\alpha^{\prime}\in S,\;\|\alpha-\alpha^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\delta_{N}\}. By definition, α\alpha is δN\delta_{N}-regional if and only if α∈SδN\alpha\in S_{\delta_{N}}. Set R¯bA,(N)=RbA,(N)∖SδN\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}=R^{A,(N)}_{b}\setminus S_{\delta_{N}}, so that ⋃b∈[N]R¯bA,(N)=Δ⁡(𝒜)∖SδN\bigcup_{b\in[N]}\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}=\Delta(\mathcal{A})\setminus S_{\delta_{N}}. Let δN′=δN​2\delta_{N}^{\prime}=\delta_{N}\sqrt{2} and define the shifted regions

R~bA,(N)=R¯bA,(N)−δN′​eb={α−δN′​eb:α∈R¯bA,(N)}.\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\;=\;\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}-\delta_{N}^{\prime}e_{b}\;=\;\bigl\{\alpha-\delta_{N}^{\prime}e_{b}:\alpha\in\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\bigr\}.

The following claim adapts the shrink-and-shift technique of [21, Lemma 3] to our setting.

Claim A.2.

The sets R~1A,(N),…,R~NA,(N)\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{N} are pairwise disjoint subsets of (1−δN′)⋅Δ⁡(𝒜)(1-\delta_{N}^{\prime})\cdot\Delta(\mathcal{A}).

Proof of Claim A.2.

Disjointness.  Suppose for contradiction that R~bA,(N)∩R~b′A,(N)≠∅\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\cap\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b^{\prime}}\neq\emptyset for some b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime}. Then there exist α∈R¯bA,(N)\alpha\in\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b} and β∈R¯b′A,(N)\beta\in\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b^{\prime}} with α−δN′​eb=β−δN′​eb′\alpha-\delta_{N}^{\prime}e_{b}=\beta-\delta_{N}^{\prime}e_{b^{\prime}}, giving ‖α−β‖=δN′​‖eb−eb′‖=δN′​2=2​δN\|\alpha-\beta\|=\delta_{N}^{\prime}\|e_{b}-e_{b^{\prime}}\|=\delta_{N}^{\prime}\sqrt{2}=2\delta_{N}. The midpoint m=12​(α+β)m=\tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta) lies in Δ⁡(𝒜)\Delta(\mathcal{A}) by convexity, so m∈RℓA,(N)m\in R^{A,(N)}_{\ell} for some ℓ\ell with ℓ≠b\ell\neq b or ℓ≠b′\ell\neq b^{\prime} (possibly both). Assuming without loss of generality that ℓ≠b\ell\neq b, closedness of RbA,(N)R^{A,(N)}_{b} and RℓA,(N)R^{A,(N)}_{\ell} yields a point α′∈RbA,(N)∩RℓA,(N)⊆S\alpha^{\prime}\in R^{A,(N)}_{b}\cap R^{A,(N)}_{\ell}\subseteq S on the segment from α\alpha to mm, with ‖α′−α‖≤‖m−α‖=δN\|\alpha^{\prime}-\alpha\|\leq\|m-\alpha\|=\delta_{N}. This places α∈SδN\alpha\in S_{\delta_{N}}, contradicting α∈R¯bA,(N)\alpha\in\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}.

Containment.  For any α∈R¯bA,(N)\alpha\in\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}, Assumption 3.6 gives αb≥2​δN>δN′=δN​2\alpha_{b}\geq 2\delta_{N}>\delta_{N}^{\prime}=\delta_{N}\sqrt{2}, so the shifted point α−δN′​eb\alpha-\delta_{N}^{\prime}e_{b} has all coordinates nonnegative and summing to 1−δN′1-\delta_{N}^{\prime}. Hence R~bA,(N)⊆(1−δN′)⋅Δ⁡(𝒜)\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\subseteq(1-\delta_{N}^{\prime})\cdot\Delta(\mathcal{A}). ∎

Since each R~bA,(N)\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b} is a translate of R¯bA,(N)\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}, Claim A.2 gives

μN−1​(Δ⁡(𝒜)∖SδN)\displaystyle\mu_{N-1}\bigl(\Delta(\mathcal{A})\setminus S_{\delta_{N}}\bigr) =∑b=1NμN−1​(R¯bA,(N))=∑b=1NμN−1​(R~bA,(N))\displaystyle=\sum_{b=1}^{N}\mu_{N-1}\bigl(\overline{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\bigr)=\sum_{b=1}^{N}\mu_{N-1}\bigl(\widetilde{R}^{A,(N)}_{b}\bigr)
≤μN−1​((1−δN′)⋅Δ⁡(𝒜))=(1−δN​2)N−1​μN−1​(Δ⁡(𝒜)),\displaystyle\leq\mu_{N-1}\bigl((1-\delta_{N}^{\prime})\cdot\Delta(\mathcal{A})\bigr)=(1-\delta_{N}\sqrt{2})^{N-1}\,\mu_{N-1}\bigl(\Delta(\mathcal{A})\bigr),

and therefore

ℙ⁡(α​ is ​δN​-regional)=μN−1​(SδN)μN−1​(Δ​(𝒜))≥1−(1−δN​2)N−1,\mathbb{P}\big(\alpha\text{ is }\delta_{N}\text{-regional}\big)=\frac{\mu_{N-1}(S_{\delta_{N}})}{\mu_{N-1}(\Delta(\mathcal{A}))}\geq 1-(1-\delta_{N}\sqrt{2})^{N-1},

where α∼Unif⁡(Δ⁡(𝒜))\alpha\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\Delta(\mathcal{A})). Setting δN=c/N\delta_{N}=c/N for c∈(0,12]c\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}], this becomes

ℙ⁡(α​ is ​δN​-regional)≥1−(1−c​2N)N−1.\mathbb{P}\big(\alpha\text{ is }\delta_{N}\text{-regional}\big)\geq 1-\left(1-\frac{c\sqrt{2}}{N}\right)^{N-1}.

∎

Corollary A.3.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.7,

lim infN→∞ℙ⁡(α​ is ​δN​-regional)≥ 1−e−c​2.\liminf_{N\to\infty}\;\mathbb{P}\!\big(\alpha\text{ is }\delta_{N}\text{-regional}\big)\;\geq\;1-e^{-c\sqrt{2}}.
Proof.

Since ln⁡(1−x)≤−x\ln(1-x)\leq-x for all x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1),

(1−c​2N)N−1≤e−c​2​(1−1/N),\left(1-\frac{c\sqrt{2}}{N}\right)^{N-1}\leq e^{-c\sqrt{2}(1-1/N)},

and taking N→∞N\to\infty yields the result. ∎

Restatement of Theorem  4.1. Consider a game GG with a finite set of exogenous states, and let srs_{r} denote the true realized state. Let αi,ts\alpha_{i,t}^{s} denote the strategy selected by player ii at time step tt given state prediction ss produced by algorithm 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG}, and let (α¯is,α¯−is)(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s}) be the unique equilibrium joint strategy profile given prediction state ss. Suppose utilities are bounded, i.e. Ui​(⋅,⋅,s)∈[0,1]U_{i}(\cdot,\cdot,s)\in[0,1] for all ss. If

𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢​(s)​[∑t=1T|Ui​(αi,ts,α−i,ts,s′)−Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,s′)|]∈o⁡(T)∀fixed ​(s,s′),\underset{\mathcal{ALG}(s)}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s},s^{\prime})-U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s^{\prime})\bigr|\right]\in o(T)\quad\forall\,\text{fixed }(s,s^{\prime}),

then 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}, which combines 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG} with successive elimination to determine an evaluation state, yields strategies satisfying

𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′​[∑t=1T|Ui​(αi,tst,α−i,tst,sr)−maxs∈𝒮⁡Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,sr)|]∈o⁡(T).\underset{\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s_{t}},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s_{t}},s_{r})-\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\,U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s_{r})\right|\right]\in o(T).
Proof of Theorem  4.1.

Step 1: Bandit Reduction. Since 𝒮\mathcal{S} is finite, we treat each state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} as an arm in a multi-armed bandit problem. The goal of successive elimination is to identify a best evaluation state, i.e. a state ss under which 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG} achieves the highest utility when evaluated at the true state srs_{r}; by Proposition 3.3 this state need not be srs_{r} itself. The key difficulty is that within a single run of 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢​(s)\mathcal{ALG}(s), the rewards

Xts:=Ui​(αi,ts,α−i,ts,sr)X_{t}^{s}:=U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s},s_{r})

are correlated across time steps tt, since 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG} is adaptive. We resolve this by redefining what constitutes a single arm pull via an epoch structure.

Notation. For each state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} write

Rs:=Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,sr)R^{s}:=U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s_{r})

for the arm’s true value, the equilibrium utility of prediction ss evaluated at the true state; RsR^{s} is free of any epoch index. Let s∗∈arg​maxs∈𝒮⁡Rss^{*}\in\argmax_{s\in\mathcal{S}}R^{s} be a best evaluation state; it need not equal srs_{r}. Write Δs:=Rs∗−Rs≥0\Delta_{s}:=R^{s^{*}}-R^{s}\geq 0 for the gaps at these values and Δmin\Delta_{\min} for the smallest positive gap. (If no gap is positive, every state is optimal and only the exploration cost below is incurred.)

Step 2: Epoch Structure. Define epochs k=1,2,…k=1,2,\ldots with lengths Tk=kT_{k}=k. Let 𝒮k⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{S} denote the set of surviving arms entering epoch kk, initialized to 𝒮1=𝒮\mathcal{S}_{1}=\mathcal{S}. In each epoch kk, for every surviving arm s∈𝒮ks\in\mathcal{S}_{k}, we run a fresh independent instantiation of 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢​(s)\mathcal{ALG}(s) over TkT_{k} rounds and compute the empirical reward

R^ks:=1Tk​∑t=1TkUi​(αi,ts,α−i,ts,sr).\hat{R}_{k}^{s}:=\frac{1}{T_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s},s_{r}).

Since each epoch uses a fresh independent instantiation, R^ks\hat{R}_{k}^{s} and R^k′s\hat{R}_{k^{\prime}}^{s} are independent across epochs k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}, recovering the independence across pulls that the bandit framework requires. Within-epoch correlations are absorbed into the single observation R^ks\hat{R}_{k}^{s}. Since Ui​(⋅,⋅,s)∈[0,1]U_{i}(\cdot,\cdot,s)\in[0,1] by assumption, R^ks∈[0,1]\hat{R}_{k}^{s}\in[0,1], and any bounded random variable is sub-Gaussian.

The epoch rewards are not identically distributed. Applied over an epoch of length TkT_{k}, the hypothesis of the theorem (with s′=srs^{\prime}=s_{r}) gives

|𝔼⁡[R^ks]−Rs|≤1Tk​𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢​(s)​[∑t=1Tk|Ui​(αi,ts,α−i,ts,sr)−Rs|]=o⁡(Tk)Tk,\bigl|\mathbb{E}[\hat{R}_{k}^{s}]-R^{s}\bigr|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{T_{k}}\,\underset{\mathcal{ALG}(s)}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T_{k}}\bigl|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s},s_{r})-R^{s}\bigr|\right]\;=\;\frac{o(T_{k})}{T_{k}},

which vanishes as the epoch index kk grows. This is a property of 𝒜​ℒ​𝒢\mathcal{ALG} on the instance, independent of the horizon TT; hence there is a constant k0k_{0}, entering the analysis only, with per-epoch bias at most Δmin/8\Delta_{\min}/8 for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0} and all s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}.

Step 3: Successive Elimination over States. We now apply the Successive Elimination algorithm of  [7] with arms 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Recall that at each epoch kk, arm ss produces the independent observation R^ks∈[0,1]\hat{R}_{k}^{s}\in[0,1]. The empirical mean of arm ss after tt epochs is

p^ts:=1t​∑k=1tR^ks,centered at ​𝔼​[p^ts]=1t​∑k=1t𝔼⁡[R^ks].\hat{p}_{t}^{s}:=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=1}^{t}\hat{R}_{k}^{s},\qquad\text{centered at }\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}_{t}^{s}]=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\hat{R}_{k}^{s}].

The algorithm maintains a surviving set 𝒮t⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S} and at each epoch tt eliminates any arm ss satisfying

p^tmax−p^ts≥ 2​αt,αt=ln⁡(c​|𝒮|​t2/δ)t,\hat{p}_{t}^{\max}-\hat{p}_{t}^{s}\;\geq\;2\alpha_{t},\qquad\alpha_{t}=\sqrt{\frac{\ln(c|\mathcal{S}|t^{2}/\delta)}{t}},

where p^tmax=maxs∈𝒮t⁡p^ts\hat{p}_{t}^{\max}=\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\hat{p}_{t}^{s}, c>4c>4 is an absolute constant, and δ=1/T\delta=1/T.

The probabilistic engine of Theorem 3 of  [7] is the tail bound Pr[|p^ts−𝔼[p^ts]|≥αt]≤e−αt2​t≤δ/(c|𝒮|t2)\Pr\bigl[|\hat{p}_{t}^{s}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}_{t}^{s}]|\geq\alpha_{t}\bigr]\leq e^{-\alpha_{t}^{2}t}\leq\delta/(c|\mathcal{S}|t^{2}) with a union bound over epochs and arms. This is Hoeffding’s inequality, whose requirements are independence and sub-Gaussian summands, both established in Step 2, and which centers the empirical mean at the average of the summands’ means; identical distribution is not among its hypotheses. Hence with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

|p^ts−𝔼⁡[p^ts]|≤αtfor all ​s∈𝒮​ and all ​t≥1;|\hat{p}_{t}^{s}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}_{t}^{s}]|\leq\alpha_{t}\qquad\text{for all }s\in\mathcal{S}\text{ and all }t\geq 1;

call this event EE.

What must be supplied is the mean control: that 𝔼⁡[p^ts]\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}_{t}^{s}] is close enough to RsR^{s}. By Step 2,

|𝔼⁡[p^ts]−Rs|≤k0t+Δmin8≤Δmin4once ​t≥8​k0/Δmin.\bigl|\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}_{t}^{s}]-R^{s}\bigr|\;\leq\;\frac{k_{0}}{t}+\frac{\Delta_{\min}}{8}\;\leq\;\frac{\Delta_{\min}}{4}\qquad\text{once }t\geq 8k_{0}/\Delta_{\min}.

With this in hand, on EE the confidence intervals cover RsR^{s} with radius αt+Δmin/4\alpha_{t}+\Delta_{\min}/4: for t≥8​k0/Δmint\geq 8k_{0}/\Delta_{\min} the best arm is never eliminated by a suboptimal arm ss, its empirical deficit being at most

p^ts−p^ts∗≤−Δs+Δmin2+2​αt< 2​αt;\hat{p}_{t}^{s}-\hat{p}_{t}^{s^{*}}\;\leq\;-\Delta_{s}+\frac{\Delta_{\min}}{2}+2\alpha_{t}\;<\;2\alpha_{t};

and a suboptimal arm ss is eliminated once 4​αt≤Δs−Δmin/24\alpha_{t}\leq\Delta_{s}-\Delta_{\min}/2, for which αt≤Δs/8\alpha_{t}\leq\Delta_{s}/8 suffices, i.e. within K∗=O⁡(ln⁡T/Δmin2)K^{*}=O(\ln T/\Delta_{\min}^{2}) epochs. Before t≥8​k0/Δmint\geq 8k_{0}/\Delta_{\min} no elimination can occur for T≥e2​k0/ΔminT\geq e^{2k_{0}/\Delta_{\min}}: an elimination requires 2​αt≤12\alpha_{t}\leq 1, hence t≥4​ln⁡T≥8​k0/Δmint\geq 4\ln T\geq 8k_{0}/\Delta_{\min}. An optimal arm may eliminate another optimal arm; this is harmless, and every surviving set contains an optimal arm.

The accounting holds at any finite TT: the initial epochs before the bias settles cost O⁡(1)O(1) rounds; the elimination phase costs

Nelim≤|𝒮|​∑k≤K∗Tk≤|𝒮|​K∗2=o⁡(T)N_{\mathrm{elim}}\;\leq\;|\mathcal{S}|\sum_{k\leq K^{*}}T_{k}\;\leq\;|\mathcal{S}|\,K^{*2}\;=\;o(T)

rounds; and the failure event ECE^{C} contributes at most δ​T=1\delta T=1.

Step 4: Bounding the Cumulative Suboptimality. Split the horizon at the end of epoch K∗K^{*} and decompose

𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′​[∑t=1T|Ui​(αi,tst,α−i,tst,sr)−maxs∈𝒮⁡Ui​(α¯is,α¯−is,sr)|]\displaystyle\underset{\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|U_{i}(\alpha_{i,t}^{s_{t}},\alpha_{-i,t}^{s_{t}},s_{r})-\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\,U_{i}(\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{s},\bar{\alpha}_{-i}^{s},s_{r})\right|\right]
≤𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′​[∑t=1T|⋯||E]+𝔼𝒜​ℒ​𝒢′​[∑t=1T|⋯||EC]⋅ℙ⁡(EC).\displaystyle\leq\underset{\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|\cdots\right|\,\Big|\,E\right]+\underset{\mathcal{ALG^{\prime}}}{\mathbb{E}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|\cdots\right|\,\Big|\,E^{C}\right]\cdot\mathbb{P}(E^{C}).

Rounds up to epoch K∗K^{*}, on EE. These number at most Nelim=o⁡(T)N_{\mathrm{elim}}=o(T), each contributing at most 11.

Rounds after epoch K∗K^{*}, on EE. By Step 3 every surviving arm ss satisfies Rs=maxs′∈𝒮⁡Rs′R^{s}=\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}R^{s^{\prime}}. If a single arm survives, the algorithm commits to it and, by the hypothesis of the theorem applied at that ss,

Appendix B Experimental Details

Conservation Security Game. The cell values record elephant counts, drawn from a study tracking 15 African elephants within Etosha National Park published on the Movebank repository [9], covering movements from 2008 to 2014. The patrol-grid overlay partitions the reserve into nine cells whose boundaries are calibrated to elephant population density and its temporal variation: regions of high and variable activity receive finer-grained cells, while persistently low-activity regions are consolidated into coarser ones. This was to ensure that the experimental setup reflects where the distribution of patrol resources would be most meaningful. We construct 396 game instances spanning February 2013 to March 2014, one per evaluation day. We average the utilities across all instances for both ETE and PTO approaches and compare across training runs for models allowed to train up until a different number of epochs.

Infrastructure Security Game. The cell values record subway ridership, drawn from New York Metropolitan Transit Authority records [19], covering 123 Manhattan stations from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2024. We construct 1098 game instances by averaging observations over 8-hour windows (approximately 3 instances per day). As with the conservation game, we average utilities across all instances for both approaches and compare across training epoch budgets.

Feature Engineering.

For each observation, we extract temporal features capturing details about the period in which the observation occurs, e.g., the month, day of week. We additionally construct WW autoregressive lag features per cell, where the ii-th lag corresponds to the value observed at that cell ii time periods prior. The full feature vector for each observation is thus 𝐱=(temporal features,vt−1,vt−2,…,vt−W)∈ℝd\mathbf{x}=(\text{temporal features},v_{t-1},v_{t-2},\ldots,v_{t-W})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where vt−iv_{t-i} denotes the ii-th lagged value and dd is the total feature dimension.

Train-Validation-Test Split.

We employ a strict temporal split to prevent data leakage. For the infrastructure game, all observations from 2024 are held out as the test set, while the pre-2024 data is partitioned into training and validation sets. For the conservation game, we analogously reserve data from February 24 2013 up until March 28 2014 for final temporal segment for testing. In both cases, we identify the set of unique time periods in the training pool and randomly assign 15% of these time periods—rather than individual rows—to the validation set. This ensures that all cells observed at a given time period fall entirely within either the training or validation fold, preventing the model from exploiting contemporaneous cross-cell information during validation.

Architecture.

The Base MLP consists of two fully connected hidden layers. The input is projected to a hidden dimension of h=256h=256, followed by Layer Normalization, a SiLU activation, and dropout with probability p=0.2p=0.2. The second hidden layer reduces the dimension to h/2=128h/2=128 with a SiLU activation, and a final linear layer projects to a single scalar output. A ReLU activation is applied at the output to enforce non-negativity, reflecting the physical constraint that state values cannot be negative. This architecture is shared across both domains. For the Conservation Security Game, the input encodes spatial cell features; for the Infrastructure Security Game, the input consists of 132 features per station — six lagged 8-hour ridership windows and a 123-dimensional station one-hot encoding — and the model is applied independently per station to predict the next ridership value.

Training Procedure.

The supervised loss is the Huber loss, which is robust to outlier values compared with mean squared error. Optimization uses AdamW with weight decay 0.010.01 and a ReduceLROnPlateau schedule that halves the learning rate after 5 epochs without improvement in validation Huber loss. The initial learning rate is η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} (Conservation) or η=0.01\eta=0.01 (Infrastructure) for PTO and ZOC, and η=5×10−4\eta=5\times 10^{-4} for KKT and Hybrid in both domains. Gaussian input noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I) with σ=0.01\sigma=0.01 is applied during the supervised updates of PTO, ZOC and Hybrid; KKT uses no input noise, and KKT and Hybrid clip gradient norms at 1.01.0. ZOC and Hybrid use regimes of R=50R=50 epochs. All models are trained for 500 epochs over 5 independent seeds. For the Infrastructure Security Game, the KKT and Hybrid models anneal the Huber regularization weight from λmax=5.0\lambda_{\max}=5.0 to λmin=3.0\lambda_{\min}=3.0 linearly over 300 epochs (for Hybrid, counted from the end of its first supervised regime), with strategic gradient steps restricted to a top-k=20k=20 station subset and up to 32 time windows sampled per epoch. In the Conservation Security Game we do not use Huber regularization in the strategic loss (λmax=λmin=0\lambda_{\max}=\lambda_{\min}=0), and up to 128 time windows are sampled per epoch.

Evaluation.

We evaluate along both statistical and strategic axes. On the statistical side, we report Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between predicted and actual values across all cell-time pairs in the test set. On the strategic side, the predicted state vector s^\hat{s} is used to construct the payoff matrices of the security game, from which a Strong Stackelberg Equilibrium (SSE) defender strategy is computed via linear programming and evaluated against the actual state ss to obtain the realized defender utility. This applies to both domains. For the Infrastructure Security Game, the test set comprises 1,098 8-hour windows across 123 stations; we report per-window utility (total utility /1098/1098) as the primary metric.

Compute. All experiments were run on a single GPU; full runs (5 seeds, 500 epochs) take approximately 1–2 hours per domain for PTO and ZOC. For the Infrastructure Security Game, KKT and Hybrid runs take approximately 3–4 hours due to per-epoch LP gradient calls via cvxpylayers. CPU-only execution is supported but substantially slower for the differentiable LP methods.

Controlled Experiments

B.1 Synthetic Conservation Security Game

Setup.

We design a synthetic security game (N=100N=100 cells, catch penalty P=10P=10) to explore when each training objective succeeds or fails, rather than to produce aggregate rankings. The exogenous state is an animal density map (non-negative, peak cell normalised to 1010). The defender receives nobs=5n_{\mathrm{obs}}=5 independent sparse noisy sweeps, each visiting 2020 of 100100 cells uniformly at random with Poisson-corrupted counts. All four methods share the same four-layer CNN (convolutional with instance normalisation, SiLU activations, Softplus output) trained with AdamW on 1,0001{,}000 synthetic scenarios for 200200 epochs.

Training objectives. PTO minimises Huber loss on predicted density and retains the final epoch. ZOC (Zero-Order Checkpointing) trains identically but evaluates downstream strategic utility on a held-out 15%15\% of training data every 2020 epochs, retaining the checkpoint that maximises that score. KKT directly maximises defender utility by backpropagating through the Stackelberg LP via cvxpylayers: the attacker’s best-response target t∗t^{*} is found by binary search (detached from the graph), the LP is re-solved for t∗t^{*} with gradients on, and exact KKT sensitivities flow back to model parameters. Hybrid alternates between 2020-epoch Huber regimes and 2020-epoch KKT regimes, reverting to the running-best checkpoint after each regime if strategic utility does not improve.

Density states are drawn from three families: (i) Gaussian blobs — 22–44 randomly placed modes (σ∈[0.05,0.25]\sigma\in[0.05,0.25]); (ii) sparse spikes — 11–66 isolated cells with non-zero value; and (iii) concentric rings. Crucially, the three families induce structurally different attacker best-response landscapes, letting us study regime-dependent behaviour rather than a single aggregate score. We present the qualitative observations below:

When does Hybrid help?

Hybrid is most effective on spatially extended multi-modal densities (Figure 5, top row), where it outperforms both ZOC and KKT alone by up to 0.80.8 utility units. The revert-to-best filter consistently accepts the KKT phase on these instances.

When does KKT alone win?

On sparse spike densities (Figure 5, second row), KKT alone achieves the highest utility. Hybrid’s revert-to-best filter which leads to rejection of some KKT updates, results in sub-optimality for this particular setting.

When does PTO or ZOC win?

On densities with two well-separated modes of unequal weight (Figure 5, third row), accuracy ends up being a very important part of determining the most dense mode. This plays an outsized role in shaping utility.

Summary.

Hybrid is the natural default for multi-modal, spatially extended densities. KKT alone dominates when the density is sparse and the best-response target is unambiguous; it can fail when the landscape is smooth or multi-modal. PTO and ZOC remain competitive when predictive accuracy and strategic utility are well-aligned, most commonly for single-dominant-mode distributions. Designing a switching criterion that conditions Hybrid’s acceptance step on the stability of t∗t^{*} rather than a scalar utility threshold is a key direction for future work.
